definition: A slight, rapid fluctuation of pitch used by singers and instrumentalists to add warmth and expressiveness to a sustained note.
origin: From Italian vibrato (vibrated), the past participle of vibrare (to vibrate), from Latin vibrare (to shake, brandish). Musicians adopted the Italian musical term into English in the 19th century.

definition: Elaborate, ornamental vocal melody featuring rapid runs, trills, and leaps, or a soprano who specialises in singing it.
origin: From Italian coloratura (coloring), from colorare (to color), from Latin color (color). The term was borrowed into German and then English in the 18th century to describe brilliantly ornamented operatic singing.

definition: A short, light opera featuring spoken dialogue, comic plots, and tuneful songs, less grand and serious than full opera.
origin: From Italian operetta, the diminutive of opera (a musical drama), meaning literally "little work." The genre flourished in mid-19th-century Paris and Vienna as a lighter, comic alternative to grand opera.
